etymology: From prune, through the Old French proignier, “to trim or lop a vine,” joined to hook; hence the vinedresser’s curved blade for cutting away the useless sprigs — a tool of husbandry, not of war.
biblical_def: A pruninghook is the small curved blade the vinedresser carries into the vineyard to lop off the sprigs that spend the vine and bear nothing. In Scripture it stands, with the plowshare, for the whole settled work of peace: iron beaten out for the field and the vine rather than for the throat of a man. Isaiah sees the day: “they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks: nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more” (Isa 2:4), and Micah is given the same word (Mic 4:3). Mark carefully what goes before it. The disarming is not the achievement of the nations but the fruit of a Person: “he shall judge among the nations, and shall rebuke many people” — and it belongs to “the last days,” when the mountain of the LORD’s house is established and all nations flow unto it (Isa 2:2). Christ reigning is the cause; beaten swords are the effect. Joel turns the figure round for the day of the LORD’s reckoning: “Beat your plowshares into swords, and your pruninghooks into spears” (Joe 3:10) — the same iron, summoned back to judgment. And Isaiah sets the hook in the LORD’s own hand: “he shall both cut off the sprigs with pruning hooks, and take away and cut down the branches” (Isa 18:5), which is the husbandry the Son describes upon His own vine: “every branch that beareth fruit, he purgeth it, that it may bring forth more fruit” (Joh 15:2).
webster_summary: A hooked, curved blade used in pruning vines and trees; in Scripture a figure of settled peace, and of the LORD’s chastening of His vine.
webster_full: PRUNINGHOOK, a hook or curved knife used in lopping the superfluous branches from vines and trees.
From prune, Old French proignier, “to trim a vine,” and hook.
Joined with the plowshare it signifies the arts of peace, as the sword and spear signify war.
Swords beaten into plowshares and spears into pruninghooks (Isa 2:4; Mic 4:3).
The figure is reversed for judgment: pruninghooks into spears (Joe 3:10).
scriptures: Isa 2:4

And he shall judge among the nations, and shall rebuke many people: and they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks: nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more.
Mic 4:3

And he shall judge among many people, and rebuke strong nations afar off; and they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks: nation shall not lift up a sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more.
Joe 3:10
Beat your plowshares into swords, and your pruninghooks into spears: let the weak say, I am strong.
Isa 18:5
For afore the harvest, when the bud is perfect, and the sour grape is ripening in the flower, he shall both cut off the sprigs with pruning hooks, and take away and cut down the branches.
corruption_summary: Isaiah’s pruninghooks are carved on the wall of the United Nations and quoted as a programme of human peacemaking — the promise stolen from its Lord and handed to diplomacy.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is a theft of the text. Isa 2:4 is the most quoted verse of secular internationalism: cast in bronze, set in gardens, printed on placards, cited by statesmen who deny every line around it. Severed from its context the verse becomes a slogan — that mankind, by treaty and goodwill and enough conferences, will disarm itself and grow out of war. Scripture says nothing of the kind. The sentence has a subject, and the subject is not the nations: he shall judge among the nations, and he shall rebuke many people, and therefore they beat their swords into plowshares. The disarming is the consequence of a King enthroned and a law going forth from Zion (Isa 2:2–3), in the last days, by His arbitration. Take away the Judge and the prophecy is not merely weakened, it is falsified; for the same prophet who wrote it also wrote of the day when the loftiness of man shall be bowed down, and the LORD alone exalted. Utopian peace without Christ’s throne is not Isaiah’s hope but Babel’s, and Joel answers it with the reverse forging — pruninghooks back into spears — for the LORD summons the nations to the valley of decision rather than to the negotiating table.

Recover the double use of the blade. Outward, it is the pledge that Christ’s kingdom really does turn weapons into implements: where the gospel goes, feuds die, hands that took up the spear take up the hook, and men sit every one under his vine and under his fig tree (Mic 4:4). That is not achieved by disarmament treaties but by conversion, and it is as certain as the mouth of the LORD of hosts that spoke it. Inward, the pruninghook is in the Father’s hand upon His own vine. He cuts off the sprigs that draw sap and bear nothing (Isa 18:5); He purges the fruitful branch that it may bring forth more fruit (Joh 15:2). The believer who feels the blade should not conclude he is being cut off; the barren branch is taken away, but the fruitful branch is purged, and the wound is the husbandman’s care, not his wrath. The hook that will one day be beaten out of the world’s spears is already at work in the vineyard of the redeemed.
roots_summary: A curved vinedresser’s blade; with the plowshare, the standing emblem of peace under Messiah’s reign.
roots_lines: Pruninghook — prune (Old French proignier, to trim a vine) + hook.
Hebrew mazmerah, the vinedresser’s lopping knife (Isa 2:4; Joe 3:10).
Paired always with the plowshare: the tools of the field against the tools of war.
Isaiah and Micah give the same oracle; Joel reverses it for judgment.
In Isa 18:5 the hook is the LORD’s own, cutting the sprigs of His vine.
usage: Spears into pruninghooks is Christ’s doing, not diplomacy’s: read the clause before it.
Joel forges the pruninghook back into a spear — the LORD can summon peacetime iron to judgment.
The pruninghook in the Father’s hand is mercy: the fruitful branch is purged, not cut off.

etymology: From the Old French musel, the snout of a beast, whence the band or cage bound over it; hence to muzzle is to bind the mouth shut, that the beast may not bite — or, on the threshing floor, may not eat.
biblical_def: To muzzle is to bind a beast’s mouth so that it cannot feed. The law forbids it at the one place where the temptation is greatest: “Thou shalt not muzzle the ox when he treadeth out the corn” (Deu 25:4). The ox was driven round the threshing floor over the heaped sheaves, his hoofs breaking the grain from the husk; the grain lay open beneath his very mouth, and a grasping master would tie that mouth shut to save a handful. God forbids it. The beast that does the work shall eat of the work. This little agricultural statute the apostle Paul takes up twice, and both times he applies it to the maintenance of gospel ministers. To the Corinthians: “For it is written in the law of Moses, Thou shalt not muzzle the mouth of the ox that treadeth out the corn. Doth God take care for oxen?” (1Co 9:9) — that is, was the statute given merely for cattle, or was it written for our sakes? He concludes, “Even so hath the Lord ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel” (1Co 9:14). To Timothy he goes further still: “For the scripture saith, Thou shalt not muzzle the ox that treadeth out the corn. And, The labourer is worthy of his reward” (1Ti 5:18) — binding Moses and the words of Christ recorded by Luke together under the one authority, the scripture.
webster_summary: To bind or cover the mouth of a beast to prevent it biting or feeding; forbidden to the ox that treads out the corn.
webster_full: MUZZLE, to bind the mouth; to fasten the mouth to prevent biting or eating.
From Old French musel, the snout of an animal, and the band bound upon it.
The Mosaic statute forbids muzzling the treading ox (Deu 25:4).
Paul twice applies the law to the support of gospel ministers (1Co 9:9; 1Ti 5:18).
The principle: he that labours in the work shall live of the work.
scriptures: Deu 25:4
Thou shalt not muzzle the ox when he treadeth out the corn.
For it is written in the law of Moses, Thou shalt not muzzle the mouth of the ox that treadeth out the corn. Doth God take care for oxen?
For the scripture saith, Thou shalt not muzzle the ox that treadeth out the corn. And, The labourer is worthy of his reward.
Even so hath the Lord ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel.
corruption_summary: The muzzled ox is the underpaid pastor — and the twice-quoted statute is also a standing rebuke to those who treat the Old Testament as a discarded husk.
corruption_paragraphs: The live misuse is a congregational one, and it is old: churches that will spend freely on the building and starve the man who feeds them from the word. The pretence is usually piety — that a minister ought to be poor, that money would corrupt him, that his reward is in heaven. Paul does not permit the argument. He grants that he himself forbore the right at Corinth, and then insists at length that it was a right, ordained of the Lord: if we have sown unto you spiritual things, is it a great thing if we shall reap your carnal things? (1Co 9:11). The muzzle can be tied in more ways than one — by the salary too small to live on, by the elder kept dependent and therefore compliant, by the arrears no one will name. A church that binds the mouth of the ox it drives is not frugal; it is under the law’s censure. The other side of the ditch is the hireling who preaches for filthy lucre, and Scripture condemns him too; but the statute before us is aimed at the master, not the beast.

The deeper service of this verse is what it proves about the Bible itself. Paul does not treat Deu 25:4 as an obsolete farming rule from a superseded covenant. He treats the very words as breathed out for the church’s instruction — for our sakes, no doubt, this is written — and he reasons from the precise wording, not merely from the general drift. That is verbal plenary inspiration argued from an ox. And in 1Ti 5:18 he sets the sentence from Moses beside “The labourer is worthy of his reward” from Luke’s Gospel and calls the pair, together, the scripture. The apostle is thus a witness that the Gospel then being written was already received as canonical alongside the law of Moses. The modern habit of dismissing the Old Testament as a husk the church has trodden out and left behind is refuted from within the New: the apostles built their doctrine of ministry, of giving, and of the canon itself upon a line about a hungry ox.
roots_summary: To bind the mouth of a working beast; forbidden by Moses, twice pressed by Paul into the doctrine of ministerial support.
roots_lines: Muzzle — Old French musel, the snout, hence the band bound upon it.
Hebrew chasam, to stop or bind the mouth (Deu 25:4).
Greek phimoo, to muzzle, to put to silence (1Co 9:9; 1Ti 5:18).
The treading ox ate of the floor he threshed; the law protected his portion.
Paul: the Lord ordained that gospel preachers live of the gospel (1Co 9:14).
usage: Thou shalt not muzzle the ox: the beast that does the threshing eats of the grain.
Paul reasons from an ox to a pastor’s wage — and calls Moses and Luke alike the scripture.
A congregation that starves its minister has tied a muzzle it will answer for.

etymology: Old English hōf, the horny casing of a beast’s foot; cognate with the German Huf. In the law the hoof is examined for its cleft, and in Exodus it stands by synecdoche for the whole animal.
biblical_def: The hoof is the horny foot of a beast, and in the ceremonial law it is the first of two marks by which Israel was to sort the clean from the unclean. The animal must part the hoof and be clovenfooted and chew the cud; one mark without the other left the creature unclean. “And every beast that parteth the hoof, and cleaveth the cleft into two claws, and cheweth the cud among the beasts, that ye shall eat” (Deu 14:6). The camel chews the cud but does not divide the hoof; the swine divides the hoof but does not chew the cud (Deu 14:8); neither may be eaten. The hoof is the outward, visible mark — the foot, the walk, the tread a beast leaves in the dust. It answers to a man’s conduct before the eyes of others, and Scripture will not let outward conduct stand alone: the swine has the parted foot and is unclean still. These distinctions were ceremonial, given to teach Israel to put difference between the holy and the profane, and they were fulfilled and set aside in Christ, being “a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ” (Col 2:17; cf. Act 10:15; Mar 7:19). The word has one other great use: standing before Pharaoh, Moses refused every partial surrender — “there shall not an hoof be left behind” (Exo 10:26).
webster_summary: The horny substance covering the feet of certain beasts; in the law, the parted hoof was one of the two marks of a clean animal.
webster_full: HOOF, the horny substance that covers or terminates the feet of certain animals, as horses, oxen, and sheep.
Old English hōf; the hoof of a clean beast must be parted and clovenfooted.
The twofold test: parting the hoof and chewing the cud (Lev 11:3; Deu 14:6).
The swine divides the hoof but chews not the cud, and is unclean (Deu 14:8).
By synecdoche, the whole beast: not an hoof left behind (Exo 10:26).
scriptures: Deu 14:6
And every beast that parteth the hoof, and cleaveth the cleft into two claws, and cheweth the cud among the beasts, that ye shall eat.
Deu 14:8
And the swine, because it divideth the hoof, yet cheweth not the cud, it is unclean unto you: ye shall not eat of their flesh, nor touch their dead carcase.
Our cattle also shall go with us; there shall not an hoof be left behind; for thereof must we take to serve the LORD our God; and we know not with what we must serve the LORD, until we come thither.
Col 2:17
Which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ.
corruption_summary: The clean-hoof laws are pressed into service as an ancient health code, and Moses’ refusal to leave a hoof behind is quietly abandoned wherever worship is negotiated with the world.
corruption_paragraphs: The common corruption of the hoof laws is to reduce them to hygiene — the notion that God forbade pork because of trichinosis and shellfish because of spoilage, so that Leviticus becomes a primitive public-health leaflet. The text gives no such reason. It gives holiness: ye shall be holy, for I am holy. The lines were drawn to teach Israel discernment and to fence her off from the nations, every meal a lesson in the difference between the holy and the profane. Reduce the law to medicine and two errors follow at once: the sabbatarian food-law movements that bind Christian consciences to a code Christ has fulfilled, and the opposite error of concluding that a merely practical rule may be discarded without reckoning with what it taught. Scripture’s own verdict is neither: the ceremony is abolished, the instruction abides. What God hath cleansed, call not thou common (Act 10:15); let no man judge you in meat or in drink (Col 2:16); yet the discernment those laws trained is now required of every believer at a higher level, in the discerning of good and evil.

The hoof’s second lesson is Moses’ before Pharaoh, and it is the regulative principle in a sentence. Pharaoh offered four compromises: sacrifice in the land, do not go far away, leave your little ones, leave your flocks. Moses answered the last of them, “there shall not an hoof be left behind; for thereof must we take to serve the LORD our God; and we know not with what we must serve the LORD, until we come thither” (Exo 10:26). Two things are in that refusal. First, whole-hearted obedience: God is not served by a negotiated remainder, and the man who keeps back a hoof has already conceded the principle. Second, and more pointed, Moses will not presume upon the worship God has not yet prescribed. He does not know what the LORD will require, and therefore he will not decide beforehand what may be spared. That is exactly the posture the regulative principle demands — that worship waits on the command of God and adds nothing of its own (Deu 12:32; Lev 10:1).
roots_summary: The horny foot of a beast; one of two ceremonial marks of cleanness, and Moses’ word for the whole undiminished offering.
roots_lines: Hoof — Old English hōf, the horny casing of the foot.
Hebrew parsah, hoof; the clean beast parteth the hoof and is clovenfooted.
The mark is outward and visible — the walk, the tread, the conduct seen of men.
Alone it never sufficed: the swine parts the hoof and is unclean (Deu 14:8).
Exo 10:26 makes the hoof stand for the whole: nothing withheld from the LORD.
usage: The parted hoof is the outward mark — and the swine proves that outward marks alone save no one.
The hoof laws taught Israel to put difference; Christ fulfilled the shadow and kept the lesson.
Not an hoof left behind: Moses would not haggle with Pharaoh over the LORD’s worship.

etymology: Old English cwidu, that which is chewed; the food a ruminant returns from the first stomach to the mouth to be chewed a second time. Hence to chew the cud, to ruminate, to turn a thing over slowly.
biblical_def: The cud is the food a ruminant beast brings up again out of its stomach to chew a second time. With the parted hoof it forms the twofold test of the clean beast in the ceremonial law, and it is the inward mark as the hoof is the outward. “Nevertheless these shall ye not eat of them that chew the cud, or of them that divide the hoof: as the camel, because he cheweth the cud, but divideth not the hoof; he is unclean unto you” (Lev 11:4). Neither mark availed without the other. The whole apparatus had one declared end, and it was not diet but discernment: “Ye shall therefore put difference between clean beasts and unclean… which I have separated from you as unclean” (Lev 20:25). The priests were charged to teach Israel that very habit — “the difference between the holy and profane” (Eze 44:23) — and every meal rehearsed the lesson until it was in the bone. That is what the cud pictures: not a glance at the word but the slow return to it, the second and third chewing, the meditating day and night by which truth is broken down and turned into strength. The ceremony is abolished in Christ; the faculty it trained is commanded still, for strong meat belongs to them “who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil” (Heb 5:14).
webster_summary: Food returned from the first stomach of a ruminant to be chewed again; hence to ruminate, to meditate.
webster_full: CUD, the food which ruminating animals return from the first stomach into the mouth to be chewed a second time.
Old English cwidu, that which is chewed; whence to chew the cud, to ruminate.
In the law it is the inward mark of the clean beast (Lev 11:3-4; Deu 14:6).
The camel chews the cud yet is unclean, wanting the parted hoof (Lev 11:4).
Figuratively, to turn a matter over in the mind; to meditate at length.
scriptures: Lev 11:4
Nevertheless these shall ye not eat of them that chew the cud, or of them that divide the hoof: as the camel, because he cheweth the cud, but divideth not the hoof; he is unclean unto you.

Ye shall therefore put difference between clean beasts and unclean, and between unclean fowls and clean: and ye shall not make your souls abominable by beast, or by fowl, or by any manner of living thing that creepeth on the ground, which I have separated from you as unclean.
And they shall teach my people the difference between the holy and profane, and cause them to discern between the unclean and the clean.
Heb 5:14
But strong meat belongeth to them that are of full age, even those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil.
corruption_summary: An age that skims has lost the chewing of the cud — and a church that will not put difference between the holy and the profane has lost what the law was given to teach.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live loss is a habit, not a doctrine. The clean beast is marked by rumination: it takes the food down, brings it up, and works it a second time until the good of it is extracted. The Christian mind was made for the same labour — the psalmist’s meditation day and night, the Bereans searching daily, the Puritan practice of taking one text into the week and returning to it until it yielded. What has displaced it is the skim: the verse-image, the clip, the plan that measures reading by chapters covered rather than truth digested, the sermon consumed at double speed and forgotten by dinner. A man may read the whole Bible in a year and chew nothing. The remedy is unfashionable and simple — less at one sitting, returned to more often, prayed over, spoken back to God, until the word is not merely swallowed but assimilated and turned into blood and bone.

The second thing to recover is what the two marks together were teaching. The camel ruminates and is unclean; the swine parts the hoof and is unclean; only where the inward and the outward agree is the beast clean. So it is with men. There is a religion of the visible foot — the correct walk, the attended service, the reputation kept — with no meditation behind it; and there is a religion of the ruminating mouth — the man full of doctrine and warm feeling whose tread in the dust betrays him. Neither is cleanness. Christ has abolished the shadow and no Christian is bound to the table of beasts (Col 2:16–17; Act 10:15), but He has not abolished the discernment the shadow trained. Ezekiel’s charge to teach the difference between the holy and the profane now falls on the eldership, and the mark of maturity in Hebrews is precisely a sense exercised by use to tell good from evil. Discrimination is not a vice to repent of; in Scripture it is a sign of growth.
roots_summary: The chewed-again food of the ruminant; the inward mark of the clean beast, and Scripture’s picture of meditation.
roots_lines: Cud — Old English cwidu, that which is chewed.
Hebrew gerah, the cud; the clean beast bringeth up and chews again.
It is the inward mark, as the parted hoof is the outward.
The camel chews the cud and is unclean still — one mark never sufficed (Lev 11:4).
Figuratively: meditation, the slow second chewing of the word of God.
usage: Chewing the cud is meditation — the truth taken down, brought up, and worked again.
The camel ruminates and is unclean: inward warmth without an outward walk proves nothing.
The ceremony is fulfilled in Christ; the discernment it trained is commanded still (Heb 5:14).

etymology: From first with the diminutive suffix -ling, denoting the young of a creature; hence the firstborn of a beast — the first male to open the matrix of herd or flock.
biblical_def: A firstling is the firstborn male of a beast, the first to open the matrix of herd or flock, and by the LORD’s claim it was never the owner’s to keep. The word enters Scripture at the first act of worship recorded after Eden: “And Abel, he also brought of the firstlings of his flock and of the fat thereof. And the LORD had respect unto Abel and to his offering” (Gen 4:4). The difference between the brothers was not agriculture but faith and blood — “By faith Abel offered unto God a more excellent sacrifice than Cain” (Heb 11:4) — and Abel gave the firstborn and the fat, the best and the first, not the leavings. Under the law the claim was formalized: every firstling male of herd and flock was to be sanctified to the LORD, put to no work, unshorn (Deu 15:19), and if clean, its blood sprinkled on the altar and its fat burned, for “they are holy” (Num 18:17). But the ass was unclean and could not be offered, and here the law preaches the gospel with terrible plainness: “every firstling of an ass thou shalt redeem with a lamb; and if thou wilt not redeem it, then thou shalt break his neck” (Exo 13:13). A lamb dies in its place, or it dies itself. There is no third way for the unclean firstling, and none for us.
webster_summary: The first produce or offspring of a beast; the firstborn of herd or flock, claimed by the LORD.
webster_full: FIRSTLING, the first produce or offspring; applied to beasts, as the firstling of a cow, a sheep, an ass.
From first and the diminutive -ling; the male that first openeth the matrix.
Abel brought of the firstlings of his flock and of the fat thereof (Gen 4:4).
Clean firstlings were sacrificed and not redeemed; they are holy (Num 18:17).
The firstling of an ass, being unclean, was redeemed with a lamb or its neck broken (Exo 13:13).
scriptures: Gen 4:4
And Abel, he also brought of the firstlings of his flock and of the fat thereof. And the LORD had respect unto Abel and to his offering:
Heb 11:4
By faith Abel offered unto God a more excellent sacrifice than Cain, by which he obtained witness that he was righteous, God testifying of his gifts: and by it he being dead yet speaketh.
And every firstling of an ass thou shalt redeem with a lamb; and if thou wilt not redeem it, then thou shalt break his neck: and all the firstborn of man among thy children shalt thou redeem.

But the firstling of a cow, or the firstling of a sheep, or the firstling of a goat, thou shalt not redeem; they are holy: thou shalt sprinkle their blood upon the altar, and shalt burn their fat for an offering made by fire, for a sweet savour unto the LORD.
corruption_summary: Abel’s firstlings are read as a lesson in generosity or in agrarian sentiment, when the text is about faith and substitutionary blood — and the ass’s broken neck refuses every soft gospel.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is moralizing. Abel’s offering is preached as a lesson in giving God your best, and Cain’s as the stinginess of a man who kept back the good fruit — a stewardship sermon lifted out of a passage about atonement. Give it its weight. Abel brought a slain firstling and its fat; Cain brought the produce of ground that God had cursed, bloodlessly, on his own terms. Hebrews does not say Abel’s sacrifice was larger, but that it was offered by faith, and that by it he obtained witness that he was righteous. The difference was not quantity of devotion but the ground of acceptance: a life laid down in the sinner’s room, received by faith, versus a worship of man’s own devising. The second corruption is the sentimental reading of the firstling of the ass — the modern instinct that recoils from the broken neck and quietly drops the verse. But the verse is the whole gospel in one sentence, and softening it costs everything.

Set the two firstlings side by side. The clean firstling was holy and could not be redeemed: its blood went to the altar, for it was the offering itself — and that is Christ, the firstborn of every creature, whose blood was never to be exchanged for another. The unclean firstling — the ass, the beast of burden, useful and dirty, exactly the sinner’s emblem — had no worth to bring to God at all. For it the law appointed one alternative and no more: a lamb dies in its stead, or its own neck is broken (Exo 13:13; Exo 34:20). No third option is offered, no improvement of the ass, no delay, no partial payment. Either substitution or death. Every Israelite child who watched a lamb led out for the family donkey was being catechized in the doctrine of particular redemption before he could read, and the same terms stand at the Judgment: Christ in your room, or your own soul answering for itself for ever.
roots_summary: The firstborn male of a beast, claimed by the LORD; the emblem of both the Lamb offered and the sinner redeemed.
roots_lines: Firstling — first + -ling; the firstborn of herd or flock.
Hebrew bekor / peter, the male that first openeth the matrix.
Abel’s firstlings and their fat were accepted; Cain’s bloodless offering was not (Gen 4:4).
Clean firstlings were not redeemed but sacrificed — they are holy (Num 18:17).
The firstling of an ass: redeemed with a lamb, or its neck broken (Exo 13:13).
usage: Abel brought the firstlings and the fat — the best and the first, and by faith.
A clean firstling could not be redeemed; it was the offering.
Redeemed with a lamb or its neck broken: the unclean firstling has no third option.

etymology: From bond (that which binds) and man; a man bound to service. In the Authorized Version it renders the Hebrew 'ebed, a servant, most often one who has sold himself for debt.
biblical_def: A bondman is a man bound to service. The Authorized Version uses the word chiefly for the Hebrew who, sinking into poverty, sold his labour to a brother until the debt was worked off. The Mosaic code hedges that condition about on every side. He is not to be treated as a chattel: “if thy brother that dwelleth by thee be waxen poor, and be sold unto thee; thou shalt not compel him to serve as a bondservant” (Lev 25:39) — he is to be as a hired servant, not ruled over with rigour (Lev 25:43). His term is fixed: “if thy brother, an Hebrew man, or an Hebrew woman, be sold unto thee, and serve thee six years; then in the seventh year thou shalt let him go free from thee” (Deu 15:12), and not empty-handed, but furnished liberally from flock, floor, and winepress. The reason given is redemption remembered: “thou shalt remember that thou wast a bondman in the land of Egypt, and the LORD thy God redeemed thee” (Deu 15:15). And there is one more provision, the loveliest in the code. If the servant will not go out because he loves his master and his master’s house, his ear is bored through with an aul at the door and he serves for ever (Deu 15:16–17). The bondslave by love, not by debt — and in Psa 40:6 the Messiah says, mine ears hast thou opened.
webster_summary: A man bound to service; in the Mosaic law, a Hebrew sold for debt, protected by statute and released in the seventh year.
webster_full: BONDMAN, a man in bondage; a servant bound to service without wages, as opposed to a freeman.
From bond, that which binds, and man; rendering the Hebrew 'ebed.
The Hebrew bondman served six years and went free in the seventh (Deu 15:12).
He might not be ruled over with rigour, nor sold as a bondman (Lev 25:42-43).
Manstealing, the seizing and selling of a man, was a capital crime (Exo 21:16).
scriptures: And if thy brother that dwelleth by thee be waxen poor, and be sold unto thee; thou shalt not compel him to serve as a bondservant:
And if thy brother, an Hebrew man, or an Hebrew woman, be sold unto thee, and serve thee six years; then in the seventh year thou shalt let him go free from thee.
And thou shalt remember that thou wast a bondman in the land of Egypt, and the LORD thy God redeemed thee: therefore I command thee this thing to day.
And he that stealeth a man, and selleth him, or if he be found in his hand, he shall surely be put to death.
corruption_summary: The charge that Scripture endorses chattel slavery collapses on the text: the law it actually gives makes manstealing a capital crime and sets the bondman free with a full hand.
corruption_paragraphs: The accusation is made constantly and it must be answered plainly, not hedged. Scripture does not endorse chattel slavery; it prescribes the death penalty for the trade that creates it. “He that stealeth a man, and selleth him, or if he be found in his hand, he shall surely be put to death” (Exo 21:16), and Paul lists menstealers with murderers and perjurers as contrary to sound doctrine (1Ti 1:10). Every man in the African slave trade — the raider, the shipper, the auctioneer, the buyer holding stolen men — stood under a capital sentence from the law he claimed to honour. The Mosaic institution is a different thing entirely: an indenture entered by a man’s own act to discharge a debt, with a fixed six-year term, release in the seventh, release at Jubilee, a liberal severance out of the master’s own goods, a prohibition of rigour, freedom for any servant maimed by his master, and a standing refusal to return a fugitive (Deu 23:15–16) — the exact reverse of the fugitive-slave laws that disgraced the Christian West. The wickedness of race-based chattel slavery is not softened by biblical precedent; it is condemned by biblical law, and by the abolitionists who read that law rightly.

The doctrine to recover from this word is the aul in the ear. The law provided a way out for the man who did not want one: “if he say unto thee, I will not go away from thee; because he loveth thee and thine house, because he is well with thee” (Deu 15:16), then his ear was bored through at the door and he served for ever — a freeman who chose bondage out of love. The Psalmist puts that language in the mouth of the Messiah: “Sacrifice and offering thou didst not desire; mine ears hast thou opened… I delight to do thy will, O my God” (Psa 40:6, 8), and Hebrews reads it of Christ coming into the world: “a body hast thou prepared me… Lo, I come… to do thy will, O God” (Heb 10:5, 7). He was under no debt, no compulsion, no necessity. He took upon Him the form of a servant (Php 2:7) because He loved the Father and loved the house, and He wears the marks of that willing bondage in His hands for ever. Every ransomed sinner is thereby made the Lord’s freeman — and, in the same breath, Christ’s servant (1Co 7:22).
roots_summary: A man bound to service; in Israel a debtor with a fixed term, in Christ a servant by love.
roots_lines: Bondman — bond, that which binds, + man.
Hebrew 'ebed, servant; Greek doulos, bondservant.
Six years' service, freedom in the seventh, and a liberal parting gift (Deu 15:12-14).
Manstealing was capital under Moses and is condemned by Paul (Exo 21:16; 1Ti 1:10).
The aul through the ear marked the servant who would not go free (Deu 15:17).
usage: Remember that thou wast a bondman in Egypt: redemption remembered makes a merciful master.
The law that regulated the bondman hanged the manstealer — Exo 21:16 ends the argument.
The aul in the ear: a servant who stays because he loves his master — and so did Christ.

etymology: From bond, that which binds, and maid, a young woman or female servant; a woman bound to service. It renders the Hebrew amah or shiphchah and the Greek paidiske.
biblical_def: A bondmaid is a woman bound to service — the female counterpart of the bondman, and under the Mosaic law protected by the same statutes. The Hebrew woman sold for debt went free in the seventh year exactly as her brother did: “if thy brother, an Hebrew man, or an Hebrew woman, be sold unto thee, and serve thee six years; then in the seventh year thou shalt let him go free” (Deu 15:12); the daughter sold as a maidservant could not be treated as a chattel but was to be dealt with as a daughter, with food, raiment, and duty of marriage secured, and free departure without money if these were denied (Exo 21:7–11). The word is used in the wider sense of household servants bought of the surrounding nations in Lev 25:44. But the great theological use of bondmaid is Paul’s. Hagar, Sarah’s Egyptian handmaid, becomes in Galatians the figure of a whole covenant: “Abraham had two sons, the one by a bondmaid, the other by a freewoman” (Gal 4:22). The son of the bondmaid was born after the flesh, the son of the freewoman by promise; the two women are the two covenants; and the apostle’s conclusion is not a suggestion but an eviction: “Cast out the bondwoman and her son” (Gal 4:30). Works-religion and grace cannot share the inheritance.
webster_summary: A woman bound to service; a female slave or handmaid — and in Galatians, the figure of the covenant of works.
webster_full: BONDMAID, a female slave, or one bound to service without wages; a handmaid.
From bond and maid; rendering the Hebrew amah and the Greek paidiske.
The Hebrew bondmaid went free in the seventh year with her brother (Deu 15:12).
The daughter sold as a maidservant was to be dealt with as a daughter (Exo 21:7-11).
Hagar the bondmaid figures the covenant from mount Sinai which gendereth to bondage (Gal 4:22-24).
scriptures: Both thy bondmen, and thy bondmaids, which thou shalt have, shall be of the heathen that are round about you; of them shall ye buy bondmen and bondmaids.
Gal 4:22
For it is written, that Abraham had two sons, the one by a bondmaid, the other by a freewoman.
Gal 4:30
Nevertheless what saith the scripture? Cast out the bondwoman and her son: for the son of the bondwoman shall not be heir with the son of the freewoman.
Gal 4:31
So then, brethren, we are not children of the bondwoman, but of the free.
corruption_summary: Hagar is enlisted as a case study in oppression and Sarah cast as the villain, so that the passage about two covenants is emptied of its doctrine.
corruption_paragraphs: The fashionable handling of Hagar reads her as the wronged woman of the story and stops there — the bondmaid as a grievance narrative, Abraham and Sarah as the guilty powerful, the God of the passage reduced to a sympathizer. Scripture’s own tenderness toward Hagar is real and should not be lost: the LORD found her by the fountain, heard the lad’s voice where he was, opened her eyes to the well, and made of Ishmael a great nation; she is the first person in Scripture to give God a name, Thou God seest me. Abraham and Sarah’s scheme to obtain the promise by the flesh was sin, and it bore bitter fruit for four thousand years. But Paul does not read the account as a case study in the abuse of the weak; he reads it as an allegory of two covenants, and he says so in as many words (Gal 4:24). Strip that out and Galatians loses its argument, which is the argument on which justification by faith alone stands or falls.

The doctrine is this. Ishmael was produced by Abraham’s own contrivance — a real son by ordinary generation, obtained by taking the promise into his own hands. Isaac was produced by promise out of a dead womb, by God alone. So the covenant from mount Sinai, considered as a way of obtaining life by doing, gendereth to bondage; and the Jerusalem which is above is free, which is the mother of us all. Every man who works to place God in his debt is a son of the bondmaid, however religious his sweat; every man who rests on Christ’s finished obedience is a son of the freewoman. And the two claims cannot cohabit in one house or one conscience: cast out the bondwoman and her son, for the son of the bondwoman shall not be heir with the son of the freewoman. That is the sharpest word in the New Testament against every scheme of grace-plus-works, and it ends where the believer’s comfort begins — we are not children of the bondwoman, but of the free (Gal 4:31; cf. Gal 5:1).
roots_summary: A woman bound to service; protected by Mosaic statute, and in Paul the figure of the covenant of bondage.
roots_lines: Bondmaid — bond + maid, a woman bound to service.
Hebrew amah / shiphchah; Greek paidiske, a maidservant.
The Hebrew bondmaid's release in the seventh year was the same as the man's (Deu 15:12).
Hagar the bondmaid: her son born after the flesh, Isaac by promise (Gal 4:22-23).
The two women are the two covenants; the bondwoman is cast out (Gal 4:24, 30).
usage: The bondmaid went free in the seventh year with her brother — the law knew no lesser release for women.
Hagar and Sarah are the two covenants: flesh-contrivance against promise.
Cast out the bondwoman: works and grace cannot inherit together.

etymology: From the Old French plege, a surety or security, through the Late Latin plebium; hence a thing deposited with a creditor as security for a debt — a pawn, a gage.
biblical_def: A pledge is the thing a debtor puts into a creditor’s hand as security for what he owes. Since the poor man’s only movable goods were the tools he worked with and the cloak he slept in, the law surrounded the taking of pledges with an extraordinary tenderness — and called that tenderness not charity but righteousness. His outer garment may be taken, but never kept overnight: “If thou at all take thy neighbour’s raiment to pledge, thou shalt deliver it unto him by that the sun goeth down” (Exo 22:26), “for that is his covering only, it is his raiment for his skin: wherein shall he sleep? and it shall come to pass, when he crieth unto me, that I will hear; for I am gracious” (Exo 22:27). His means of living may not be touched at all: “No man shall take the nether or the upper millstone to pledge: for he taketh a man’s life to pledge” (Deu 24:6). His door may not be forced: the creditor must stand outside and let the man bring out his own pledge, that he not be shamed in his own house (Deu 24:10–11). The widow’s raiment is wholly exempt (Deu 24:17). And the restoring of the pledge at sundown “shall be righteousness unto thee before the LORD thy God” (Deu 24:13). Eliphaz accuses Job of taking a pledge from his brother for nought (Job 22:6); Ezekiel makes restoring the pledge a mark of the just man (Eze 18:7, 16); Amos indicts men who lie down at the altar on garments taken to pledge (Amo 2:8).
webster_summary: Something given or deposited as security for a debt; in the law, hedged about with strict protections for the poor debtor.
webster_full: PLEDGE, something put in pawn; a thing deposited with a creditor as security for the payment of a debt.
From Old French plege, a surety; whence also pledge, to pawn or engage.
The poor man's raiment taken to pledge must be restored before sundown (Exo 22:26).
Neither millstone may be taken to pledge, for it is the man's life (Deu 24:6).
Restoring the pledge is reckoned righteousness before the LORD (Deu 24:13).
scriptures: If thou at all take thy neighbour's raiment to pledge, thou shalt deliver it unto him by that the sun goeth down:
Deu 24:6
No man shall take the nether or the upper millstone to pledge: for he taketh a man's life to pledge.
In any case thou shalt deliver him the pledge again when the sun goeth down, that he may sleep in his own raiment, and bless thee: and it shall be righteousness unto thee before the LORD thy God.
Thou shalt not pervert the judgment of the stranger, nor of the fatherless; nor take a widow's raiment to pledge:
corruption_summary: The pledge laws are claimed as proof-texts by movements that want debt abolished and lending indicted; the law does neither — it holds the debt and hedges the debtor.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors run at this law from opposite sides. The first is the modern reading that turns these statutes into a manifesto against lending and property, as though God’s answer to poverty were the cancelling of obligation and the shaming of the creditor as such. The law says otherwise. It never denies that the debt is owed, never forbids taking a pledge, never treats the lender as a criminal for lending; it takes the obligation seriously enough to secure it, and then draws hard lines the creditor may not cross — not the millstone, not the widow’s cloak, not the threshold of a man’s house, not the night. The second error is the harder one and is committed by respectable men: the reduction of this law to sentiment, a nice suggestion for the kind-hearted. Moses forecloses that reading in one clause — restore the pledge before sundown, and it shall be righteousness unto thee before the LORD thy God. It is not generosity; it is justice, and the failure of it is not stinginess but sin, with the poor man’s cry going up to a God who says I will hear; for I am gracious.

The live application is not far to seek: the lending trade built precisely on what the law forbids — interest rates that take a man’s life to pledge, terms designed so the poor never redeem the garment, the seizure of the very tools by which a debt might have been paid, the collector at the door of a house he has no business entering. Amos saw the same men worship: they lay themselves down upon clothes laid to pledge by every altar (Amo 2:8) — devout on a bed of stolen cloaks. Ezekiel names the restoring of the pledge among the marks of the just man who shall surely live (Eze 18:7, 16). And behind the whole law stands the reason a redeemed people are to keep it: the Israelite was himself a poor debtor whose surety paid what he could not, and the LORD who says I am gracious has heard the cry of the naked and covered them with a better garment than the one restored at sundown.
roots_summary: A security deposited for a debt; the Mosaic law fences its taking with protections for the poor and calls the restoring of it righteousness.
roots_lines: Pledge — Old French plege, a surety, security, gage.
Hebrew chabol / abot, a thing pawned or bound over for debt.
The garment restored by sundown; the millstone never taken at all (Exo 22:26; Deu 24:6).
The creditor stands abroad; he may not enter the debtor's house (Deu 24:10-11).
Restoring the pledge is righteousness before the LORD, not mere kindness (Deu 24:13).
usage: He shall have his cloak again by sundown — the poor man’s bed is not a creditor’s asset.
Take not the millstone to pledge: seize a man’s trade and you have seized his life.
Restoring the pledge is called righteousness, not charity — the law leaves no room for sentiment.

etymology: From the Greek sardinos, said to be named from Sardis in Lydia, where the stone was found or traded; a deep blood-red carnelian. This entry treats the Revelation 4 throne-vision word; for the breastplate stone see sardius.
biblical_def: The sardine stone is the deep blood-red carnelian, and in the Authorized Version the phrase belongs to one place above all others — the throne room of heaven. John is called up through the open door and sees no form and no face, only light and colour: “And immediately I was in the spirit: and, behold, a throne was set in heaven, and one sat on the throne” (Rev 4:2). “And he that sat was to look upon like a jasper and a sardine stone: and there was a rainbow round about the throne, in sight like unto an emerald” (Rev 4:3). Mark what John does not describe. There is no attempt at a face, no human likeness, no portrait of God — only the flash of two stones and the arc of a third. The jasper is clear and white as crystal (Rev 21:11), the light of holiness and untouchable purity; the sardine is red as blood, the fire of justice and the price of redemption. Holiness and judgment together, and encircling both a rainbow, the sign sworn to Noah that the flood shall not return — mercy bending round the throne of the Judge. The same stone appears as sardius in the sixth foundation of the New Jerusalem’s wall (Rev 21:20). Before this throne the elders cast their crowns and say, “Thou art worthy, O Lord” (Rev 4:11).
webster_summary: A deep blood-red carnelian; in Rev 4:3 the colour under which the One seated on heaven’s throne appeared to John.
webster_full: SARDINE STONE, a precious stone of a deep blood-red colour; the carnelian or sard.
Greek sardinos, said to be named from Sardis in Lydia.
In Rev 4:3 it describes the appearance of Him that sat upon the throne.
It is paired with the crystal-clear jasper, and encircled by an emerald rainbow.
The same stone stands as sardius in the sixth foundation of the city wall (Rev 21:20).
scriptures: Rev 4:2
And immediately I was in the spirit: and, behold, a throne was set in heaven, and one sat on the throne.
Rev 4:3
And he that sat was to look upon like a jasper and a sardine stone: and there was a rainbow round about the throne, in sight like unto an emerald.
The fifth, sardonyx; the sixth, sardius; the seventh, chrysolite; the eighth, beryl; the ninth, a topaz; the tenth, a chrysoprasus; the eleventh, a jacinth; the twelfth, an amethyst.
Rev 4:11
Thou art worthy, O Lord, to receive glory and honour and power: for thou hast created all things, and for thy pleasure they are and were created.
corruption_summary: The throne vision is mined for gemstone symbolism and crystal lore, when its point is that John saw colour and light and no likeness at all — and that the throne is occupied.
corruption_paragraphs: Two live misuses attach to this stone. The first is the trade in gemstone mysticism — birthstones, chakras, crystals charged with energies — which finds in Rev 4:3 and Rev 21:20 a biblical veneer for a thoroughly pagan practice. Scripture never assigns power to a stone. The jasper and the sardine are John’s only available vocabulary for a glory that has no earthly likeness; the stones are borrowed for their light, not credited with virtue. The second and subtler misuse is a devotional one: the modern appetite for a God who can be pictured, felt, and made familiar. John, given the nearest look at heaven any man in Scripture received, reports no face. He gives colour, fire, sound, and a rainbow, and nothing that a painter could set on canvas — which is precisely the second commandment holding at the highest altitude. The vision that most tempts us to imagine is the vision that most firmly refuses the image.

Read the colours as the text sets them. Jasper: clear, crystalline, white — the unapproachable holiness of God, the light no man can approach unto. Sardine: blood-red — His justice, and the blood by which that justice was satisfied, so that the Lamb standing in the midst of the throne looks as it had been slain. Rainbow, in sight like unto an emerald: the covenant sign given after the flood, the sworn mercy of God, drawn as a complete circle round the whole throne. Holiness, judgment, and covenant mercy, and none of the three at the expense of the others. And the first thing the vision establishes is not a colour but a fact: a throne was set in heaven, and one sat on the throne. The seat is not empty and never has been. Everything that follows in the book — seals, trumpets, vials, beast, harlot, and the last enemy — is read from a chapter that begins with the occupied throne, and the elders’ response is the only fitting one: crowns cast down, and Thou art worthy, O Lord.
roots_summary: The blood-red carnelian of Rev 4:3, describing the appearance of Him that sat upon heaven’s throne.
roots_lines: Sardine stone — Greek sardinos, from Sardis in Lydia; a deep red carnelian.
Rev 4:3 is its one occurrence: the look of Him that sat on the throne.
Paired with the jasper — blood-red justice beside crystal-clear holiness.
The emerald rainbow encircles both: covenant mercy round the throne of the Judge.
The same stone is the sixth foundation of the city wall, there called sardius (Rev 21:20).
usage: Like a jasper and a sardine stone: holiness in white light, justice in blood-red fire.
John saw colour and no countenance — the throne vision refuses the image.
The rainbow bends clean round: mercy encircles the throne, it does not merely stand beside it.

etymology: Through the Latin organum from the Greek organon, an instrument or implement of any kind. In the Authorized Version it renders the Hebrew ugab, a pipe or reed instrument blown with the breath — not the keyed pipe organ of later ages.
biblical_def: The organ of the Authorized Version is the Hebrew ugab: a pipe, reed, or flute, sounded by the breath. The English word is used in its old and wide sense — organum, simply an instrument — and the reader should be plain with himself that the church pipe organ, with its keyboards, bellows, and ranks of stops, is a mediaeval and later invention nowhere named in Scripture. The word occurs four times. It appears at the very first mention of music in the Bible, in the line of Cain: “his brother’s name was Jubal: he was the father of all such as handle the harp and organ” (Gen 4:21) — music, like metalwork and city-building, is a common grace given early and given even to a cursed line. Job sets it among the pleasures of the wicked who prosper: “They take the timbrel and harp, and rejoice at the sound of the organ” (Job 21:12); and then, stripped bare, he turns the same instrument to grief: “My harp also is turned to mourning, and my organ into the voice of them that weep” (Job 30:31). Its last appearance is in the great summons of praise: “Praise him with the timbrel and dance: praise him with stringed instruments and organs” (Psa 150:4). The pipe is thus a creature — used for revelry, used for lament, and finally lifted up to praise the LORD.
webster_summary: In the Authorized Version, the ugab, a pipe or wind instrument sounded by the breath — not the keyed church organ.
webster_full: ORGAN, an instrument or implement; hence, a wind instrument of music sounded by pipes.
Latin organum, Greek organon, an instrument of any sort.
In Scripture it renders the Hebrew ugab, a pipe or reed blown with the breath.
Jubal was the father of such as handle the harp and organ (Gen 4:21).
The keyed church organ with bellows and stops is a later invention, not the biblical ugab.
scriptures: Gen 4:21
And his brother's name was Jubal: he was the father of all such as handle the harp and organ.
They take the timbrel and harp, and rejoice at the sound of the organ.
My harp also is turned to mourning, and my organ into the voice of them that weep.
Praise him with the timbrel and dance: praise him with stringed instruments and organs.
corruption_summary: The AV word is regularly read back into the church organ loft, and Psa 150 is then used to end an argument about worship that it was never speaking to.
corruption_paragraphs: The plain error first: the Bible does not mention the pipe organ. The ugab was a breath-blown pipe, closer to a flute or reed than to anything in a chancel, and the AV translators used organ in its old broad sense of instrument. Preachers who cite Psa 150:4 to defend the instrument in the corner of their own sanctuary have made an anachronism do the work of an argument, and the argument is weaker for it. The same anachronism runs the other way when a man denounces the organ as an unbiblical intrusion by pointing at Gen 4:21 and the line of Cain, as though Jubal’s parentage condemned music itself. It does not. Music is a common grace, given early, given even through a cursed line, and God has never disowned a good gift because a wicked man handled it first — Job took up the same pipe for mourning, and the Psalter takes it up for praise.

The question that actually matters is the regulative principle: in corporate worship, what God has commanded is required, and what He has not commanded is not permitted. That principle is this dictionary’s standard, and it is held with full seriousness by brethren who have come to different conclusions about instruments. Some confessional Reformed churches judge that instrumental accompaniment belonged to the temple service, appointed by the commandment of David and the prophets, and passed away with the altar and the priesthood; they sing the Psalms unaccompanied, and their argument is a serious one made from the shadow-and-substance reasoning of Hebrews. Others judge that the New Testament’s command is to sing — psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, making melody in the heart (Eph 5:19; Col 3:16) — and that the manner of assisting that singing is a circumstance ordered by Christian prudence, not an element added to worship. Neither party is defending an appetite for entertainment, and neither ought to be caricatured. What both must resist is the modern instinct that decides the question by preference, atmosphere, and effect on the crowd, which is not the regulative principle at all but its opposite (Deu 12:32; Lev 10:1).
roots_summary: The AV’s rendering of the Hebrew ugab, a breath-blown pipe; four occurrences, from Jubal to Psa 150.
roots_lines: Organ — Latin organum, Greek organon, an instrument of any kind.
Hebrew ugab: a pipe or reed sounded by the breath, akin to a flute.
Four occurrences: Gen 4:21; Job 21:12; Job 30:31; Psa 150:4.
Jubal, of Cain's line, is the father of all such as handle the harp and organ.
The keyed church pipe organ is a later invention and is not this word.
usage: The AV’s organ is the ugab, a breath-blown pipe — not the instrument in the loft.
Job’s organ was turned into the voice of them that weep: the same pipe serves mirth and mourning.
Psa 150:4 will not settle a worship question it was never asked.
